transcript:
Meeting header: 2025-06-10 15:00 PT / Duration: 52m
Attendees: Jordan Kim (Redwood AE), Priya Shah (Redwood SE), Liam O'Connor (Redwood SE), Evelyn Park (BlueStone Director ML), Marcus Li (BlueStone Platform), Nadia Gomez (BlueStone Security), Tam Tran (BlueStone Data Scientist)

Summary: Quick product walkthrough focused on model catalog guidance for open models, interpreting bench numbers in the console, and how routing/compatibility matrices affect latency and cost. Customer is evaluating options for a private routing policy and potential dedicated nodes for 24/7 inference on healthcare triage use cases.

Topics covered: model families and tradeoffs, console benchmark tiles, hardware compatibility matrix, routing/policy examples (latency-first vs cost-first), caching and KV-cache implications, pilot scope and SLOs.

-- Transcript --
00:00 Jordan Kim: hey everyone thanks for joining, I see we have the core team from BlueStone, hi Evelyn, Marcus, Nadia, Tam, thanks for making time. real quick agenda is a 35-minute demo of the catalog + console benches and then 15 for q&a. sound good?
00:14 Evelyn Park: yep that works for me, curious about the latency numbers, and also how to read the quantization and hardware compatibility.
00:24 Marcus Li: and I'll want to understand how the routing policies show up — we have peak windows where latency must be under 120ms p95.
00:36 Jordan Kim: totally, that's exactly what we'll demo — how to pick models for p95 vs cost, and the console tips for creating a route that favors latency in region A and cost in off-peak region B.
00:50 Priya Shah: hi all — quick intro from me, I'm Priya, I run SRE/bench work at Redwood, I'll walk through the benchmark tiles and live demo a quick K-V cache scenario.
01:02 Tam Tran: quick note, our prompts are long — averages 1.2k tokens per request, so sequence length matters.
01:12 Priya Shah: that's important — some kernels perform better at longer seqs, and quantization can change perf characteristics. we'll show that in the bench.
01:26 Liam O'Connor: small caveat on transcription — sometimes the console labels per-token latency as "token ms" which is an average sample, not the p95; watch the p95 box.
01:38 Jordan Kim: ok demo start — opening the model catalog, filter: open-source models, sorted by redwood-verified latency on A100 (region us-west-2)
01:56 Priya Shah: you'll notice three columns: throughput/latency profile, quality score (based on eval sets), and compatibility matrix. the compatibility shows hardware tested and quantization supported. sometimes it says "int8 supported on ampere" but not on t4 — that's expected.
02:22 Tam Tran: hmm the compatibility grid lists "KV cash" under caching, that's a transcription bug — should be KV cache.
02:30 Jordan Kim: yep our console has a few typos in the beta text — thanks for catching that.
02:36 Priya Shah: jumping to the benchmark tile for the 'OpenLM-Med-7B' variant — latency p50/p95, token ms, and cost-per-1k tokens are shown. notice the drop when enabling dynamic batching for throughput workloads.
02:58 Marcus Li: can you show what happens if we pin model to dedicated capacity in us-east-1? our infra is there.
03:12 Priya Shah: switching the view — dedicated capacity changes the bench estimator: it factors in reserved throughput, predictable KV cache hit rates, and a slightly lower variance on p95. console projects a 10-18% lower tail latency for pinned dedicated pools.
03:34 Evelyn Park: is that because of fewer noisy neighbors or different kernel selection?
03:40 Priya Shah: both — dedicated pools are isolated, and the runtime picks kernels tuned for that hardware profile; plus we can favor different batching windows.
03:52 Jordan Kim: here's the compatibility matrix for two model variants: OpenLM-Med-7B (fp16/int8) and OpenL-Mini-7B (int8 only). see the hardware rows — A100, H100, T4 — and the green/yellow icons. green means validated, yellow means "experimental".
04:18 Tam Tran: we have regulatory constraints — can Redwood show us an on-prem or private deployment equivalence?
04:26 Jordan Kim: yes, the Private option shows a similar catalog but the console adds an extra column: "deployment compatibility (VPC/on-prem)" and available kernels there are slightly different. we can run a compatibility validation as part of pilot.
04:40 Nadia Gomez: on security, does the console bench store sample prompts or payloads in the cloud? we need to ensure PHI isn't retained.
04:50 Jordan Kim: good question — console benches use anonymized synthetic prompts unless you explicitly upload a sample set. for pilot we recommend providing an anonymized set or running the bench in your VPC private deployment so nothing leaves your environment.
05:06 Marcus Li: show us the routing policy UI you mentioned earlier — we want to send traffic to lower-latency variants for premium requests and cost-optimized variants for async jobs.
05:20 Priya Shah: opening routing policies — here's a rule: if route.tag=="premium" then region=us-east-1, model_family=OpenLM-Med-7B, else region=us-west-2 and model_family=OpenL-Mini-7B. you can set fallback to a smaller family if capacity is exhausted.
05:42 Jordan Kim: note that fallbacks can be "graceful" meaning we keep the same schema and attempt to rerank to preserve quality; it's not just a blind swap.
05:52 Tam Tran: how does caching interact — if we cache prefixes on the edge, will fallback still honor cached tokens?
06:02 Priya Shah: yes, prefix/KV cache is orthogonal to model variant — the runtime will attempt cache hits first, then rehydrate KV cache aligned with the model's key schema; occasional mismatches can happen if model tokenizers differ.
06:22 Marcus Li: tokenizer mismatches worry me — can we see an example?
06:28 Priya Shah: sure — quick demo: two models with different BPE vocab sizes produce different tokenization on the same prompt; the console bench shows a delta in token count and projected cost.
06:40 Jordan Kim: here's an annotation in the bench "tokenization delta: +12 tokens" — multiply that by request volume and you get cost differences.
06:52 Evelyn Park: on quality score — what's the baseline? our prompts are clinical triage, not general chat.
06:58 Priya Shah: great point. the catalog quality score is based on public evals; for clinical triage we recommend running an eval with your held-out set. the Optimize toolkit can run those evals and tie alerts to regressions.
07:18 Tam Tran: could we integrate our own eval dataset into the console?
07:24 Jordan Kim: yes — Optimize supports custom eval sets; you can upload via API or UI and run scheduled evals, then tie thresholds to rollouts.
07:32 Nadia Gomez: about compliance, if we do private deployment and KMS integration, can you confirm logs/audit retention? we need 7 years for some records.
07:44 Jordan Kim: Redwood Private can route logs to your SIEM via S3/Cloud Storage with configurable retention; for hosted we have default retention windows and an add-on for extended retention. we'll send the compliance doc.
08:00 Marcus Li: can you run a quick bench showing int8 vs fp16 on a long sequence and the impact on p95 and cost?
08:12 Priya Shah: running a simulated bench now — note this is a console estimator, we can run your sample in a pilot for more accurate numbers.
08:20 [screen share noise, brief silence]
08:32 Priya Shah: results: OpenLM-Med-7B fp16 — p95: 220ms (us-east-1, H100), cost per 1k tokens: $1.12. OpenLM-Med-7B int8 — p95: 185ms, cost per 1k tokens: $0.68. however quality delta measured on a small eval set was: accuracy -1.8% (clinical intent).
09:04 Tam Tran: that -1.8% is concerning for triage. what's the usual approach?
09:10 Priya Shah: many customers use mixed strategy: use int8 for lower-criticality flows and keep fp16 for high-risk prompts, or use a reranker ensemble to catch regressions.
09:24 Jordan Kim: we can also suggest quantization-aware finetuning if you want to close that -1.8% gap; Redwood Optimize can recommend that and coordinate with partner labs.
09:38 Evelyn Park: latency budgets — earlier Marcus said p95 <=120ms. these numbers are higher — what levers do we have?
09:46 Priya Shah: levers: 1) choose smaller architecture (but quality tradeoff), 2) move to dedicated/colocated hardware in your region, 3) tune batching windows and KV cache warms, 4) apply model distillation or use a fast reranker pipeline.
10:06 Marcus Li: can you quantify benefit of dedicated in numbers for our traffic pattern?
10:12 Priya Shah: based on similar customers, dedicated in same region shaved p95 by 20-30% and reduced variance; with aggressive cache warming p95 can drop another 10-15% for repeated prompts. we'll include rough numbers for BlueStone in the follow-up.
10:28 Jordan Kim: a quick note on billing: hosted per-token pricing vs Dedicated reserved capacity — the console has a cost estimator that can project monthly spend for given RPS and token distribution.
10:40 Tam Tran: show the estimator for our sample: 200 RPS average, 1.2k tokens.
10:46 Priya Shah: plugging numbers — hosted with a mix of fp16/int8 shows $Xk/month (redacted in demo), dedicated with 1 committed pool and burst covers shows 35% lower unit cost in our projection. exacts in the pricing doc we will send.
11:12 Nadia Gomez: anything about PII/PHI redaction in the console?
11:18 Jordan Kim: we offer pre-request redaction hooks and also post-response retention controls. for private deployments you own the keys and logs.
11:28 Evelyn Park: one more thing — the compatibility matrix mentions kernel "fast-attn-v2" as experimental on H100. what's the risk?
11:36 Priya Shah: experimental means validated in internal tests but not yet on all SMs; we support fallbacks, so for critical traffic we wouldn't route to experimental kernels unless you opt in.
11:48 Marcus Li: ok can you put a note in the follow-up about fallback behavior and how rollbacks are triggered automatically?
11:56 Jordan Kim: will do.
12:00 [brief cross talk about shared deck link]
12:12 Jordan Kim: wrapping up — recap: we'll send pricing and a dedicated capacity proposal, run a latency bench with your prompts, and provide compliance docs. proposed pilot scope: 4-week pilot, dedicated pool in us-east-1, 50k requests/day synthetic, integrated Optimize evals.
12:36 Evelyn Park: sounds good. let's do the pilot if benchmarks look acceptable.
12:42 Nadia Gomez: please include SOC2 scope and encryption details in the packet.
12:46 Jordan Kim: yes — action items in the calendar invite. thanks everyone.
12:52 Meeting end.
